Enki and Ninmah

Wheel of Heaven Translation

The Sumerian human-creation text: gods grind clay, place breath/word into it, and Enki and Ninmah contest over crafting bodies and assigning fates

Direct Direct Established or uncontested across mainstream sources, or a direct description of the project itself. Framework Framework Foundational premise of the Wheel of Heaven framework. Explicit in the Raëlian canon; not endorsed by mainstream scholarship. Inferred Inferred A reasonable reading of comparative material — not stated literally, but consistent with the source. Speculative Speculative Interpretive synthesis or hypothesis that goes beyond what any single source states.

An English translation of the Sumerian composition Enki and Ninmah (ETCSL 1.1.2), produced from the ETCSL composite transliteration. The composition opens with the antediluvian period when the lesser gods toiled at digging canals; Namma the primordial mother brings their lament to Enki, who instructs the grinding of clay above the abzu to create humans to bear the gods' labor; Ninmah and Enki then contest over the assignment of fates to defective bodies. The text is the Mesopotamian counterpart to Genesis 1-2 on human crafting, and pairs with Atraḫasīs on the humans-as-relief-of-divine-toil motif. Per-line commentary documents lexical decisions, ETCSL philological options, and cross-corpus links to the Hebrew Bible (Gen 1-2, Job 10:8-9), Atraḫasīs, and Enūma Eliš VI. The Wheel of Heaven's first Sumerian translation.

Chapter 1

Enki and Ninmah — humans crafted from clay; the defective-births contest

1
In those days, in those days when heaven and earth had been [fashioned each from the other];
𒌓 ud 𒊑𒀀𒋫 re-a-ta 𒌓 ud 𒀭 an 𒆠𒁉𒋫 ki-bi-ta 𒁀𒀭𒁶𒈠𒁀 ba-an-[dim2-ma-ba] ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 1

The composition opens with the canonical Sumerian once-upon-a-time formula ud re-a-ta — literally 'from those days', the stock primordial-time opener of Sumerian mythological narrative. The triple-temporal opener of vv 1-3 (ud re-a-ta / ĝi6 re-a-ta / mu re-a-ta) — 'in those days / in those nights / in those years' — is editorially-deliberate, structurally invoking a long-ago register that Foster, Jacobsen, Black et al., and ETCSL all preserve as 'in those days'. The cross-corpus ANE primordial-time-opener type includes Akkadian inūma (Enūma Eliš: enūma eliš lā nabû šamāmū — 'when on high heaven had not been named') and Hebrew be-reshit (Gen 1:1) and be-yom asot YHWH Elohim (Gen 2:4b). See overlay entry ud-re-a-ta-once-upon-a-time-formula.

The phrase an ki-bi-ta ba-an-dim2-ma-ba is the Sumerian heaven-and-earth-separation cosmogonic-formula. The crux is the suffix -bi-ta on ki — '(from) its (counterpart)', the reciprocal-ablative. Modern scholarly consensus (Jacobsen The Treasures of Darkness 1976 pp. 167-168; Kramer Sumerian Mythology; Lambert Babylonian Creation Myths 2013 ch. 9) reads the line as naming a creation-by-separation cosmology: heaven and earth begin undifferentiated and are separated. The wider Sumerian-Akkadian separation-cosmogony tradition — Enūma Eliš IV.137-140 (Marduk splits Tiamat to make heaven and earth); Gilgameš, Enkidu, and the Netherworld prologue (lines 8-13, 'after heaven had been separated from earth'); KAR 4 — supports this reading. Cross-corpus to Gen 1:6-8 (the raqia separates waters from waters); see overlay entry an-ki-bi-ta-heaven-and-earth-separation-cosmogony and existing central entry raqia. Brackets [...] mark restored text per the ETCSL convention preserved by WoH: see overlay entry lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard.

2
in those nights, in those nights when heaven and earth had [been fashioned each from the other];
𒈪 ĝi6 𒊑𒀀𒋫 re-a-ta 𒈪 ĝi6 𒀭 an 𒆠𒁉𒋫 ki-bi-ta 𒁀𒀭𒁶𒈠𒁀 /ba\-[an-dim2-ma-ba] ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 2

Second member of the triple-temporal opener (see commentary at v 1). The ĝi6 (night) variant doubles the temporal opener of v 1; the parallel structure is a standard Sumerian poetic-rhetorical device. The -bi-ta ba-an-dim2-ma-ba construction recurs verbatim — the separation-cosmogony formula is doubled across vv 1-2. The /ba\ marker indicates the sign is damaged but securely-read; per the WoH convention this is silently collapsed in the prose (see overlay entry lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard).

3
[in those] years, in the years when [destinies had been decreed];
𒈬 [mu 𒊑𒀀𒋫 re]-a-/ta\ 𒈬 mu 𒉆 nam 𒁀𒋻𒊏𒁀 ba-[tar-ra-ba] ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 3

Third member of the triple-temporal opener. The line introduces the verbal-idiom nam tar — 'to cut a destiny / decree a fate' — the foundational Sumerian theological-conceptual-category that will saturate the composition. Nam (destiny / fate) combines with tar (to cut) in the metaphor of cutting a destiny: the divinatory-and-juridical sense of tar — to cut a decision, to determine by separation. See central entry nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus for the cross-corpus Sumerian-Akkadian sibling-cluster (Sumerian nam + the Akkadian šīmtu destiny-lexeme) and the partial-functional-cognate Hebrew goral (lot, portion; Lev 16:8-10; Josh 14-19; Ps 16:5; Prov 16:33).

4
when the Anuna had been born;
𒉣𒈾𒆤𒉈 [^da]-/nun\-na-ke4-ne 𒁀𒌅𒌓𒁕𒀀𒁀 ba-tu-ud-da-a-ba ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 4

First occurrence of the collective-noun for the great gods: a-nun-na — Anuna. The Anuna are the senior-body of the Mesopotamian pantheon, presided over by An (sky-god), Enlil (storm-god of Nippur), and Enki (wisdom-god of the abzu). The Sumerian-source form Anuna is preserved per the ETCSL convention; the Akkadian-form Anunnakū / Anunnaki (with the variously-analyzed -ki/-ke₄ suffix), widely-popularized in modern literature, is documented at the central entry anuna-collective-of-great-gods-cross-corpus. Cross-corpus to the wider ANE divine-assembly tradition: Hebrew bnei Elohim (Gen 6:1-4; Job 1:6, 2:1, 38:7; Ps 82:1); Ugaritic pḫr ʾilm; see existing central entry bnei-elohim-yarinu and digir-sumerian-divine-lexeme-cross-corpus. The DINGIR-determinative ^d (the cuneiform-classifier prefix on divine names) is preserved in the translit field and dropped in the i18n.en prose per the overlay convention dingir-prefix-prose-drop-convention. The damage-but-readable marker /\ around nun is silently collapsed.

5
when the mother-goddesses had been taken in marriage;
𒀭𒂼𒀭𒈹 ^dama-^dinana 𒉆𒂠 nam-NIR.PA-še3 𒁀𒌇𒀀𒁀 ba-tuku-a-ba ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 5

The compound ama-Inana is read here as a class-noun for the mother-goddesses (the plural-collective rather than a proper-name 'Ama-Inana' or an Inana-epithet); see overlay entry ama-inana-mother-goddesses-class-noun. Modern Sumerologist consensus (Jacobsen The Harps that Once 1987 pp. 151-152; Kramer-Maier Myths of Enki 1989 pp. 32-33; Black et al. Literature of Ancient Sumer 2004 p. 215) supports the collective reading from the verb-agreements in vv 5-7 (taken-in-marriage, distributed, pregnant-and-giving-birth — all naturally collective). The sign-string nam-NIR.PA is preserved in capitals in the ETCSL composite because the cuneiform-to-Sumerian phonetic-reading is uncertain; the meaning is securely 'marriage'.

6
when the mother-goddesses had been distributed throughout heaven and earth;
𒀭𒂼𒀭𒈹 ^dama-^dinana 𒀭 an 𒆠𒀀 ki-a 𒁀𒆷𒀀𒁀 ba-ḫal-ḫal-la-a-ba ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 6

The mother-goddesses are distributed an ki-a — 'throughout heaven and earth'. The collective-action confirms the class-reading at v 5 (see overlay entry ama-inana-mother-goddesses-class-noun).

7
when the mother-goddesses, having […], had become pregnant and given birth;
𒀭𒂼𒀭𒈹 ^dama-^dinana […] 𒁀𒀀𒄫 ba-a-peš 𒅇𒌅𒁕𒀀𒁀 u3-tud-da-a-ba ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 7

The lacuna […] preserves the ETCSL editorial-apparatus convention (see overlay entry lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard). The verbs peš ('to be pregnant, thick, fat') and tud ('to give birth') saturate the line with female-fertility-and-birth vocabulary, consistent with the mother-goddesses-class reading at vv 5-6.

8
when the food-rations of the gods, … …, had been bound to their dining-hall;
𒀭 diĝir 𒉻𒈠𒁉 kurum6-ma-bi 𒀀 A X X 𒁉𒂠 unu2^?-bi-še3 𒁀𒀊𒆟𒀀 ba-ab-keše2-a-> ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 8

First major occurrence of diĝir — the Sumerian foundational divine-class lexeme; see the project's first Sumerian-source central entry digir-sumerian-divine-lexeme-cross-corpus, with bidirectional sibling-links to the existing Hebrew central entries elohim-as-translation, el-shaddai, and anokhi-elohei-X-avikha-ancestral-god-formula. The DINGIR-sign (𒀭) is itself an eight-pointed star — the cuneiform pictograph of heaven / star / sky — and functions both as common-noun ('a god') and as orthographic-determinative on divine names (the ^d prefix preserved in the translit field). The Sumerian diĝir is functionally-cognate with Akkadian ilum and Hebrew el / Elohim; the three lexemes form the project's first cross-language divine-class vocabulary-cluster.

Kurum6 names food-rations — the daily-bread the gods are entitled to from the temple-economy. The line introduces the gods-as-laborers / rationed-workers framing that the composition will develop: the senior-gods have food-rations bound to their dining-hall (unu2), but they are also the ones bearing the toil at the canals (v 9). The cross-corpus link to Atraḫasīs I (the gods' rations and toil) is documented at central entry du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus. The X X markers preserve illegible cuneiform signs per the lacuna convention.

9
the senior gods stood overseeing the work, while the lesser gods bore the toil.
𒀭 diĝir 𒊹𒊹 šar2-šar2 𒆥𒂷 kiĝ2-ĝa2 𒀠𒁻𒄀𒌍 al-sug2-ge-eš 𒀭 diĝir 𒌉𒌉 tur-tur 𒌅𒈝 du2-lum 𒅎𒅍𒅍𒂊𒉈 im-il2-il2-e-ne
Notes Verse 9

The senior-vs-junior god distinction is structurally-foundational. Diĝir šar2-šar2 (lit. 'the numerous/great gods') = senior-gods; diĝir tur-tur (lit. 'the small gods') = lesser-gods. The distinction reflects the wider Mesopotamian theological-hierarchy: in Atraḫasīs I the Anunnaki (senior gods, Akkadian-form of the Sumerian Anuna; see central entry anuna-collective-of-great-gods-cross-corpus) preside while the Igigi (junior laboring gods) bear the toil, which leads them to revolt and motivates the human-creation. The Sumerian Enki and Ninmah version does not deploy the Igigi name but the same structural-logic is present: senior-gods supervise, junior-gods toil, and humans are created to relieve the junior-gods' burden.

Du2-lum is the foundational Sumerian divine-toil lexeme and the cognate of the Akkadian dullu / dullum — one of the few clear loanwords from Sumerian into Akkadian. The du-lum / dullu keyword is the central technical-term of the humans-relieve-divine-toil topos that runs through Enki and Ninmah and saturates Atraḫasīs Tablet I. See central entry du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus, with cross-corpus thematic-link to Hebrew avodah, sevel, and mas oved (existing central entry mas-oved-corvee-labor-institutional-vocabulary-cross-corpus).

10
The gods were dredging the watercourses <of clay>, and were heaping up its earth at Harali.
𒀭 diĝir 𒀀𒇉 id2 𒅎 im> 𒂄𒂄𒅇𒉈 dun-dun-u3-ne 𒁉 saḫar-bi 𒊏𒇷 ḫa-ra-li 𒅎𒁾𒁾𒁉𒉈 im-dub-dub-be2-ne ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 10

First occurrence of the foundational human-creation substance: im — clay. The lesser-gods are dredging the id2 (watercourses, canals) and heaping up the saḫar (earth, silt) at Harali. The dredging-and-heaping-of-clay is the canonical Mesopotamian image of corvée-labor in the wet-Mesopotamian-marshland; the same labor that humans will be created to take over.

Im is the Sumerian foundational clay lexeme — the substance of human-creation across the Sumerian-Akkadian-Hebrew creation traditions. The cross-corpus sibling-cluster spans Sumerian im / Akkadian ṭiṭṭu / Hebrew afar (dust; Gen 2:7) and chomer (clay; Job 10:9; Isa 64:8); see central entry im-sumerian-clay-of-human-creation-cross-corpus, with bidirectional sibling-links to the existing Hebrew central entries adam-adamah and afar-va-efer-creatural-humility. The Hebrew Joban verb qaratz ('nip off, pinch'; Job 33:6: me-chomer qoratzti gam-ani — 'from clay I was nipped off') is the lexical-and-functional cognate of the Sumerian kir3-kir3 ('nip off', deployed at Enki and Ninmah v 32 of the SIG7-EN/SIG7-HI birth-goddesses pinching pieces from the abzu-clay).

Harali is preserved as a toponym; the location is uncertain — possibly a real geographic region in the western/southern Sumerian periphery associated with precious metals (Hallo 1987; Potts 1997 p. 165), possibly a mythic-cosmographic primordial-mound. See overlay entry harali-mythic-toponym-source-of-clay.

The ETCSL composite marker > after im and the editorial-supply in the English are preserved per the overlay convention lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard.

11
The gods, grinding the clay, kept complaining about this life.
𒀭 diĝir 𒅎 im 𒄯𒄯𒊑𒉈 ar3-ar3-re-ne 𒍣𒁉 zi-bi 𒅗 inim 𒀀𒀭𒈠𒃻𒊑𒉈 am3-ma-ĝar-re-ne
Notes Verse 11

Line 11 is one of the most-discussed cruxes in Sumerian literature. The Sumerian zi-bi inim am3-ma-ĝar-re-ne admits two principal readings with named-scholarship divided.

(i) The complain-about-life reading — ETCSL's English; Black et al. Literature of Ancient Sumer 2004. Parses zi-bi inim ĝar as the idiomatic 'place words about their life' = 'complain about life'. Zi governs the abstract sense 'life'; inim ĝar governs the sense 'voice grievance'. The reading fits the narrative-flow of vv 8-15 (the gods toil, then weep; the lament motivates Enki's intervention).

(ii) The breath-into-clay creation-summary reading — Jacobsen The Harps that Once 1987 p. 153; Lambert Babylonian Creation Myths 2013 pp. 330-345; Bottéro-Kramer Lorsque les dieux faisaient l'homme 1989 pp. 188-192; Foster Before the Muses 3rd ed. 2005 p. 156 (variable). Parses the same string as 'placed breath / life-word into it' (the clay): the gods, grinding the clay, put breath/life-word into it — a proleptic-summary of the human-creation that the rest of the composition will describe in detail. The reading takes zi in its physical sense 'breath' (the basic lexical-meaning; see central entry zi-sumerian-breath-of-life-cross-corpus) and inim as a creator-word ('the divine speech-act that animates'). The reading creates an exact-parallel with Gen 2:7's va-yipach b-apav nishmat chayyim ('and he breathed into his nostrils the breath of life') — made explicit by Lambert and Jacobsen.

The WoH translation retains the Translator's surface 'kept complaining about this life' (ETCSL reading) for the i18n.en text and surfaces the breath-into-clay alternate reading here in commentary with the Gen 2:7 cross-corpus parallel. The line is one of the corpus's clearest sites of creator-breathes-life-into-clay comparative-mythology; the cross-corpus link is documented at the central entry zi-sumerian-breath-of-life-cross-corpus with bidirectional sibling-link to the existing Hebrew central entry neshamah-chayim. See also overlay entry zi-inim-line11-breath-into-clay-vs-complain-about-life-crux for the philological detail.

12
At that time, the one of broad understanding, the maker, the one who brings into being all the senior gods —
𒌓𒁀 ud-ba 𒄑𒌆𒉿 ĝeštug2 𒂼 daĝal 𒄷𒄭 mud 𒀭 diĝir 𒊹𒊹 šar2-šar2 𒅅𒅅 ĝal2-ĝal2
Notes Verse 12

Enki's introductory-epithet-cluster: ĝeštug2 daĝal ('broad understanding, wide-of-ear'), mud ('the maker / creator'), and ĝal2-ĝal2 ('the one who brings into being'). The ĝeštug2 daĝal epithet — literally 'wide ears' — names wisdom as a capacity-for-listening, characteristically Sumerian (the ear is the seat of wisdom in the Sumerian metaphorical-imagination). Enki's epithets across the composition emphasize his craftsmanship-and-wisdom function; see central entry an-enlil-nudimmud-cosmic-triad-cross-corpus on the Nudimmud epithet of Enki (vv 26, 47) and on the cosmic-triad An / Enlil / Enki-Nudimmud.

13
Enki, in the deep engur, in the flowing subterranean waters, the place into whose interior no god can peer in wonder —
𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 ^den-ki-ke4 𒇉 engur 𒌋 buru3 𒀀𒋩𒊏 a-sur-ra 𒆠 ki 𒀭 diĝir 𒈾𒈨 na-me 𒊮𒁉 šag4-bi 𒅆𒂍 u6 𒉡𒌝𒈨 nu-um-me
Notes Verse 13

Enki's cosmographic-domain: the engur (subterranean fresh waters) and the a-sur-ra (flowing subterranean waters). The lines deploy three closely-related Sumerian cosmographic-lexemes — abzu (v 31), engur (here), a-sur-ra (here) — for the subterranean fresh-water cosmos that is Enki's domain at Eridu. The three terms are not strictly synonymous: abzu names the cosmographic-region as a whole and as Enki's temple-domain; engur names the watery-mass itself; a-sur-ra names the flow or spring-water.

This is the foundational cross-corpus cosmographic-vocabulary cluster. The Sumerian-Akkadian-Hebrew sibling-cluster: Sumerian abzu / engur / a-sur-ra ↔ Akkadian apsû (loanword from Sumerian; personified in Enūma Eliš as Tiamat's husband) ↔ Hebrew tehom (cosmographic deep, demythologized from Tiamat; Gen 1:2; Gen 7:11; Ps 33:7) ↔ Akkadian tiāmtu / Tiamat (the salt-sea cosmos; the slain dragon-goddess in Enūma Eliš). The Heidel-Westermann-Tsumura tehom-Tiamat etymological-debate is documented at the central entry abzu-engur-sumerian-subterranean-deep-cross-corpus, with bidirectional sibling-link to the existing Hebrew central entry tehom.

The phrase ki diĝir na-me šag4-bi u6 nu-um-me — 'the place into whose interior no god can peer in wonder' — emphasizes Enki's abzu as a primordial-secret-domain inaccessible even to the other gods; the cosmographic-secrecy of Enki's domain is a recurring motif across the Enki-cycle.

14
was lying on his bed, sunk in sleep, and would not rise.
𒆠𒈿𒉌 ki-nu2-ni 𒉌𒈿 i3-nu2 𒅇 u3 𒆪 ku 𒉡𒌝𒍣𒍣 nu-um-zi-zi
Notes Verse 14

Enki sleeps in his sleeping-quarter (ki-nu2) and does not rise. The image of the sleeping-wise-god who must be awakened to address a crisis is recurrent across the Mesopotamian Enki-and-Ea tradition; the awakening-by-mother (vv 17-24, where Namma carries the gods' tears to her son and rouses him) is the composition's narrative-pivot.

15
The gods broke into tears; they raised a lament, saying:
𒀭 diĝir 𒀀𒅆𒊏 er2-ra 𒅎𒉻𒉻𒉈 im-pad-pad-ne 𒀀𒉪 a-nir 𒅅 ĝal2 𒉌𒀝 i3-ak 𒅎𒈨𒉈 im-me-ne
Notes Verse 15

The gods' lament. Er2 (tears) and a-nir (lament) are paired lexemes saturating the composition's vv 15-23 lament-and-appeal section. Cross-corpus to Atraḫasīs I.300-340 (the gods' lament motivates Mami's deliberation and the human-creation) and to Gen 6:6 (the Yahwistic-source's va-yinnachem YHWH... va-yitatzev el-libbo — 'YHWH was grieved and pained in his heart'; existing central entry not yet on this; flagged for future).

16
"As for him who lies sleeping there, <as for him> who does not rise from his bed —
𒇽 lu2 𒆪𒊏 ku-ra 𒉌𒈿𒀀𒊏 i3-nu2-a-ra 𒆠𒈿𒁉 ki-nu2-bi 𒉡𒌝𒍣𒍣 nu-um-zi-zi->
Notes Verse 16

The gods' direct-speech complaint addressed to Namma about Enki's persistent sleep. The angle-bracket editorial-supply is preserved per the overlay convention lacuna-bracket-convention-sumerian-mesopotamian-project-standard.

17
Namma, the foremost mother who gave birth to all the senior gods,
𒀭𒇉𒆤 ^dnamma-ke4 𒂼 ama 𒅆𒁺 palil 𒅇𒌅 u3-tud 𒀭 diĝir 𒊹𒊹𒊏𒆤𒉈 šar2-šar2-ra-ke4-ne
Notes Verse 17

Namma is the Sumerian primordial mother-goddess — the ama palil u3-tud diĝir šar2-šar2-ra-ke4-ne ('foremost mother who gave birth to all the great gods'). She is the mother of Enki (addressed throughout the composition as ama-ĝu10 — 'my mother') and is associated with the abzu (the subterranean fresh waters; v 31). The Namma-Tiamat cognate-debate is documented at the central entry namma-primordial-mother-goddess-tiamat-comparandum: older comparative-Sumerology (Jacobsen The Treasures of Darkness 1976 pp. 110-116; Lambert Babylonian Creation Myths 2013 ch. 9) often identified Sumerian Namma with Akkadian Tiamat as both being primordial-mother-deities associated with the cosmic-watery-deep; more recent scholarship (Wiggermann RlA) is more cautious — the functional parallel is strong but the etymological-cognate-status is not secure. The WoH translation does not pre-resolve the cognate-debate. The Sumerian-source form Namma is preserved (ETCSL standard); the older Anglophone form Nammu is documented in commentary.

The line names the gods as Enki's handiwork — šu dim2-dim2-ma-zu — emphasizing Enki's creator-function and motivating Namma's appeal: Enki, the maker of the gods, must intervene to relieve their distress.

Namma's appeal proper begins. The lexeme na-aĝ2-kug-zu — wisdom — is the Sumerian foundational wisdom-lexeme (parsing nam — abstract-class-noun marker + kug — pure, holy + zu — knowledge: 'the pure-knowing' / 'the abstract-class-of-pure-knowing'). The Hebrew comparandum chokhmah (wisdom; Prov 1-9; Job 28; widely-attested) names the same functional-conceptual category; Akkadian nēmequ (wisdom; in Ludlul bel nemeqi — 'I will praise the lord of wisdom', the Akkadian Job-of-Babylon) is the Akkadian-form. The cross-corpus wisdom-vocabulary cluster spans the Sumerian-Akkadian-Hebrew traditions and will be elaborated in subsequent Mesopotamian translations.

The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 23

The pivotal command in Namma's appeal: 'fashion X so that the gods may be released from their toil!' The crux is the noun-phrase kiĝ2-sig10 dim3-me2-er-e-ne-ke4. ETCSL's token-gloss reads kiĝ2-sig10 as 'late afternoon meal' — but the natural literal reading 'evening meal of the gods' makes poor narrative-sense (how would fashioning an evening meal release the gods from their toil?). Four scholarly reading-camps: (i) the substitute-laborer reading (Black et al. Literature of Ancient Sumer 2004; ETCSL English): a 'substitute' or 'replacement-worker' — humans — fashioned to take over divine toil. (ii) Jacobsen's create-worker reading (The Harps that Once 1987 p. 153): 'create work for the gods' or 'fashion the laborer for the gods' — a similar functional reading. (iii) The literal evening-meal reading (Foster Before the Muses 3rd ed. 2005 p. 156): retains the literal 'late-afternoon meal of the gods' and reads the verse as an obscure ritual-instruction. (iv) The 'menial-work' reading (Falkenstein and older Anglophone scholarship): paraphrastic 'do the daily-work for the gods'. The WoH adopts reading (i) — 'fashion a substitute for the gods (?)' — following Black et al. and ETCSL, with the (?) flag preserving the philological uncertainty. See overlay entry kig-sig-line23-substitute-vs-evening-meal-crux.

This is the composition's humans-fashioned-to-relieve-divine-toil command — the foundational cross-corpus motif documented at the central entry du-lum-dullu-divine-toil-relieved-by-humans-cross-corpus. The cross-corpus parallel at Atraḫasīs I.190-217 is direct: the senior-gods deliberate, the wise-god (Ea / Enki) intervenes, humans are created from clay to relieve the toil. Hebrew comparanda: avodah, sevel, and the mas oved corvée-labor institutional-vocabulary (existing central entry mas-oved-corvee-labor-institutional-vocabulary-cross-corpus).

The thigh-slapping gesture is a recurring Mesopotamian deliberation-pondering gesture, attested in royal-inscriptions and cult-texts.

Jacobsen reads 'Sigensigdu and Sigenshudu' (conjectural); Kramer-Maier read 'Imma-en and Imma-hi' under an alternative imma-vocalization. The lexeme me-dim2 — 'form, articulation, limbs' — is one of the composition's recurring craftsman-vocabulary keywords; it covers both the abstract sense 'form' and the concrete sense 'limbs/body'. The lexeme recurs at vv 28, 32, 54, 83, 133.

The line is a strong cross-corpus parallel to Gen 1:26-27 (na'aseh adam b-tzalmenu — 'let us make adam in our image, after our likeness'); see existing central entry elohim-as-translation for the cross-corpus divine-self-reference at human-creation, and the planned future entry on Gen 1:26-27 tzelem v-demut.

Notes Verse 30

Enki's instruction to Namma. Zub-sig3 (Sumerian-lemma dusu; Akkadian tupšikku) is the earth-carrying basket / corvée-labor-basket — the iconic Mesopotamian symbol of the laborer's burden. The image is widely-attested across Mesopotamian iconography: the kudurru boundary-stones depict the king carrying the dusu on his head; the Ur-Nammu stele and the Gudea cylinders depict king-and-laborers carrying the basket. Binding the corvée-basket upon the human-creature is the iconographic-equivalent of transferring-the-toil from gods to humans. See central entry zub-sig-dusu-corvee-basket-cross-corpus, with cross-corpus link to Hebrew sevel (burden; Isa 9:3, 10:27, 14:25; Ps 81:7) and the wider Hebrew avodah / sevel labor-vocabulary cluster.

31
When you have mixed the heart of the clay that is over the abzu —
𒊮 šag4 𒅎 im 𒌋𒅗 ugu 𒍪𒀊𒅗 abzu-ka 𒅇𒈬𒂊𒉌𒅔𒊹 u3-mu-e-ni-in-šar2
Notes Verse 31

The abzu — Enki's subterranean fresh-water domain — and the clay that lies over it: the foundational cosmographic-and-material locus of human-creation. Enki instructs Namma to mix the im ugu abzu-ka — 'the clay that is over the abzu', the wet-clay-mud at the cosmographic-boundary-zone between the subterranean fresh waters and the earth's surface. This is the specific material from which humans are crafted.

The cross-corpus link to Gen 2:7 is foundational: the Hebrew text has va-yitzer YHWH Elohim et ha-adam afar min ha-adamah ('and YHWH Elohim formed the human, dust from the ground'), with the immediately-preceding v 2:6 v-ed yaaleh min ha-aretz v-hishqah et kol-pnei ha-adamah ('and a mist / spring rose up from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground'). Both creation-stories locate the human-creation-substance at the boundary-zone between subterranean-water and earth-surface — the wet-clay-mud where deep-water and dry-ground meet. The conceptual-parallel is documented in Westermann Genesis 1-11 (1984) and Sparks Ancient Texts for the Study of the Hebrew Bible (2005). See central entries abzu-engur-sumerian-subterranean-deep-cross-corpus and im-sumerian-clay-of-human-creation-cross-corpus, with bidirectional sibling-links to the existing Hebrew central entries tehom, adam-adamah, and afar-va-efer-creatural-humility.

The birth-goddesses (SIG7-EN and SIG7-HI; see overlay entry sig7-en-sig7-hi-birth-goddesses-uncertain-vocalization) nip off (kir3-kir3) pieces of the clay from the abzu-clay; Namma herself gives it form (me-dim2 ĝal2). The Sumerian verb kir3-kir3 — 'to nip off, pinch off' — is the lexical-and-functional cognate of Hebrew qaratz at Job 33:6: hen ani k-fikha la-El me-chomer qoratzti gam-ani — 'behold, I am, as you are, before the El, from clay I was nipped off (= pinched out)'. This is one of the corpus's clearest cross-corpus verb-cognates: the same craftsman's-gesture of pinching off pieces of clay appears in both the Sumerian creation narrative and the Hebrew Joban poetry. See central entry im-sumerian-clay-of-human-creation-cross-corpus for the substance-and-verb cross-corpus cluster (Sumerian im + kir3-kir3 ↔ Hebrew chomer + qaratz).

The Sumerian birth-ritual-vocabulary is well-documented (Stol Birth in Babylonia and the Bible 2000).

Šag4-bi ba-ḫul2 — 'his heart was glad/joyful' — the creation-completion-joy formula. The closest cross-corpus parallel is Gen 1:31 (va-yar Elohim et kol-asher asah v-hineh tov me'od — 'and Elohim saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good'); the divine-satisfaction-at-creation-completion is a cross-corpus topos. See existing central entry vayar-tov.

Notes Verse 45

The post-creation banquet — ĝišbun (cult-meal, ceremonial-banquet). The motif of gods-banquet-after-creation is the canonical Sumerian-Akkadian creation-closure: Enūma Eliš VI.69-79 has the great gods banqueting after Marduk's human-creation; Atraḫasīs I closes with a banquet-sequence. Cross-corpus to Hebrew Bible creation-completion-and-sabbath (Gen 1:31-2:3) — the closure-pattern is functionally-parallel though the Hebrew develops rest rather than banquet as the closing-motif.

Notes Verse 47

The Sumerian-Akkadian cosmic-triad: An (sky-god), Enlil (storm-god of Nippur), Nudimmud (epithet of Enki). The three senior-gods join the post-creation banquet, roasting holy kids (maš kug) as ritual-meal. Nudimmud (^dnu-dim2-mud) is one of Enki's foundational epithets, meaning approximately 'the one who fashions / the begetter / the creator'; the epithet emphasizes Enki's craftsman-and-creator function. See central entry an-enlil-nudimmud-cosmic-triad-cross-corpus. The cross-corpus Akkadian-form Anu / Enlil / Ea triad is the Akkadian-side parallel; the Hebrew Bible's divine-council tradition (see existing central entries bnei-elohim-yarinu, el-elyon, el-shaddai) is the functional Hebrew-side parallel.

Notes Verse 51

The flagship Sumerian-only theological-keyword: me. The lexeme names the divine offices / cosmic functions / archetypal cultural-patterns — the powers and ordinances of the structured-cosmos. No clean Akkadian, Hebrew, or English cognate exists; the closest Akkadian comparandum is parṣū (rites, ordinances), but the Sumerian me has a cosmographic-scope and a transferable-power aspect (cf. Inana and Enki, the me-list-of-civilizational-offices) that parṣū lacks. See central entry me-sumerian-divine-offices-cosmic-functions. The lexeme is preserved untranslated as me in the WoH translation.

The line's structural-pivot: the gods identify Enki as the master of both the me (the cosmic-offices) and the nam tar (the destiny-decreeing) — both foundational Sumerian theological-categories. Cf. central entry nam-sumerian-destiny-fate-cross-corpus.

Notes Verse 52

The drunken-contest setup: Enki and Ninmah drink beer (kaš) and their hearts grow ul (swell with joy, become giddy). The motif of the drunken-deliberation-leading-to-creation-contest is editorially significant: the contest of vv 53-101 (Ninmah fashions defective creatures; Enki finds destinies for them; the contest reverses; Enki fashions Umul; Ninmah cannot match it) is conducted under the influence. The Sumerian motif parallels — at a comparative-mythology level — Inana and Enki (where Inana steals the me from a drunk Enki) and various ANE drunken-divine-decision motifs. The motif has no direct Hebrew Bible cross-corpus parallel (Hebrew Bible mythology does not develop drunken-divine-decision topoi); the closest Greek-tradition comparandum is the Hephaestus-and-Dionysus creating-creatures-while-drinking topos (mentioned in the editorial-intake at the Translator's draft).

Notes Verse 57

Enki's contest-acceptance: 'I will counter-balance (la2) your destiny-decree.' The verb la2 — the contest-balance verb — recurs at the composition's closing v 132 (where Enki declares 'Ninmah, may your work be counter-balanced!'). The la2 verbal-construction is contested: ETCSL reads 'undo'; Jacobsen reads 'counter-balance / match'; Foster preserves the literal 'hang in the balance'. The WoH adopts the counter-balance reading following Jacobsen and the narrative-context — the contest is one of matching, not undoing: Enki finds a destiny-and-social-role for each of Ninmah's six defective creatures rather than dismissing them. Notes Verse 59

The first defective creature: the weak-handed man. The catalogue of vv 59-78 lists six (or seven, with manuscript variants) defective creatures Ninmah fashions; for each, Enki decrees a destiny and assigns a social-role. The catalogue is aetiological: it provides divine-origin-explanations for the social-roles of disabled, atypical, or unusual humans. The catalogue's editorial-stance is strikingly inclusive: the defectives are not rejected but integrated into society through divine-decreed destinies. See overlay entry lu2-gi-sushuru-sasade-nugam-weak-handed-disabled. The composition's catalogue is comparable to the medical-omen šumma izbu tradition (the monstrous-birth-omens) but reframes the defectives' fate from disaster to integration.

The blind-musician aetiology. Nam-nar — 'the art of music; the office of the nar' (Sumerian for musician; Akkadian nāru) — is allotted to the blind man. The blind-musician profession is widely-attested in Mesopotamian (and wider ANE / Greek) tradition: Homer's Demodokos in Odyssey 8; the blind Greek prophets Teiresias and Phineus; the rabbinic tradition of blind-men-gifted-in-song. See Anne Kilmer RlA s.v. Musik. The aetiology integrates blindness into society through a culturally-valued profession.

The unique-in-this-composition disease-demon Namtar. The Sumerian string nam-tar appears in the composition in the abstract-destiny sense at vv 3, 37, 46, 51, 55, 57, 78, 105, 107 (where it is the foundational divine-action verb); at v 71 uniquely it appears in the proper-name sense: Namtar the disease-demon, associated with plague and untimely death. Enki bathes the water-dripping man with a mu7-mu7 (incantation-water; ritual-purification) and drives the namtar-demon out of his flesh — a healing-exorcism. See overlay entry namtar-disease-demon-vs-destiny-parsing-crux for the dual-parsing convention. Cross-corpus to the wider Mesopotamian disease-demonology: Lamaštu, Pazuzu, Asakku, Sebettu (the seven evil winds); see Wiggermann Mesopotamian Protective Spirits 1992.

Infertility is a recurring biblical theme (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah; cross-corpus to the patriarchal-matriarchs-infertility narratives). The Sumerian aetiology gives the infertile-woman a productive social-role rather than treating infertility as a curse.

Notes Verse 77

Naming the genitally-atypical individual as the tiru — the third-gender palace-and-temple courtier — of Nibru (Sumerian-source form of the Nippur toponym). The Sumerian-Akkadian tiru / girseqû is a documented third-gender palace-and-temple role; see overlay entry tiru-third-gender-courtier-palace-attendant. The wider Mesopotamian third-gender cult-vocabulary includes the kurgarra, assinnu, and galaturra (male-bodied ritual-performers in Inana's cult); the Hebrew comparandum saris (eunuch; 2 Kgs 9:32; Esth 1:10; Isa 56:3-5; Matt 19:12) is functionally-parallel but not philologically-cognate.

Nibru is the Sumerian-source form; the Anglicized Nippur derives via Akkadian and Greek. See central entry nibru-nippur-cuneiform-cross-corpus. Nippur is the religious-and-political center of Sumer, the cult-city of Enlil and the location of the E-kur temple (see central entry ekur-house-of-the-mountain-enlil-temple-cross-corpus).

Notes Verse 101

The composition's most-discussed conceptual-category: the neither-living-nor-dead liminal-being. Ninmah's verdict on Umul: lu2 til3-la in-nu lu2 ug5-ga in-nu — 'is not a living man, is not a dead man'. The Sumerian-Akkadian liminal-being category is well-attested across the demonological-and-medical corpus (the Akkadian eṭemmū ghosts; the rabiṣu lurkers; the mukīl rēš lemutti bearers-of-evil). Umul belongs to no living-category and no dead-category — Enki's contest-creature is structurally-unprecedented. See overlay entry lu2-til-la-lu2-ug-ga-neither-living-nor-dead.

The verdict is the contest's structural-resolution: Ninmah concedes that Enki's creation falls outside any social-role-integration she can devise. The composition's narrator-statement at v 140 will confirm — Ninmah could not rival the great lord Enki.

The WoH adopts the counter-balance reading following Jacobsen and the narrative-context. The verb's la2-construction at v 57 (Enki's offer to counter-balance Ninmah's destiny) and at v 132 (Enki's contest-closing counter-balance declaration) frames the entire contest as a matching-and-balancing enterprise, not a winner-take-all defeat. Šir3 — 'song, hymn' — and nam-dub — 'the scribal art / the office of the tablet-writer'. The reference may be to the composition itself as a song-of-the-scribal-art, performed in the temple-school context.

139
"The gods who heard this — let Umul build (?) […] and act on my behalf in my house!"
𒀭 diĝir 𒄑 ĝiš 𒌇𒀀𒁉 tuku-a-bi 𒌓𒈬𒌌 u4-mu-ul du3^? […] 𒂍𒈬 e2-ĝu10 𒀝𒂊 ḫe2-ak-[e] ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 139

Enki's final disposition for Umul: assigned to build / act / function in Enki's house. Even the neither-living-nor-dead creature receives a divine-assigned-role — in Enki's own domestic-economy. The closure is editorially-significant: no creature is wasted in the Sumerian creation-economy; all are placed.

140
Ninmah could not rival the great lord Enki.
𒀭𒎏𒂊 ^dnin-maḫ-e 𒂗 en 𒃲 gal 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆤 ^den-ki-ke4 𒍠 zag 𒉡𒈬𒉌𒅔𒁺 nu-mu-ni-in-ša4 ◑Partial back-renderingThe source transliteration carries editorial restorations, damaged-sign markers, or uncertain readings the OGSL mapper could not fully resolve. The cuneiform shown is rendered for everything the mapper could map — treat as a reading aid, not an attested tablet score.
Notes Verse 140

The narrator's contest-resolution statement. Zag nu-mu-ni-in-ša4 — 'she did not rival him at the side'. The contest is decided in favor of Enki; Ninmah cannot match Umul. The resolution is final and is the composition's narrative-pivot toward the closing-doxology of v 141.

141
O father Enki, sweet is your praise!
𒀀𒀀 a-a 𒀭𒂗𒆠 ^den-ki 𒍠𒊩𒍪 za3-mi2-zu 𒄭𒂵 dug3-ga
Notes Verse 141

The composition's doxological-closing formula. Za3-mi2 — praise — is the foundational Sumerian doxological-praise lexeme, deployed in the canonical closing-formula of many Sumerian compositions: a-a [Divine-Name] za3-mi2-zu dug3-ga — 'O father / lord [Divine-Name], sweet is your praise'. The formula closes most of the Enki-cycle compositions (Enki and the World Order, Enki and Ninhursaĝa, Inana and Enki), the Inana-cycle compositions, several of the temple-hymns, and various cult-poems. See central entry za-mi-doxological-praise-formula-sumerian-cross-corpus for the cross-corpus parallels to Akkadian tanattu and Hebrew tehillah / hallel / barukh. The 'sweet is your praise' (dug3-ga) epithet parallels Hebrew naim (Ps 135:3, 147:1). The DINGIR-determinative ^d is preserved in the translit field; the divine-name Enki without prefix in the prose per the overlay convention dingir-prefix-prose-drop-convention.

Contents

    Wheel of Heaven is an open, multilingual reading of the ancient world's creation traditions — Raëlian, biblical, Mesopotamian, and others — through a single working hypothesis: that the beings called Elohim were a small advanced human civilization that came here, designed life on Earth, and left a record in the religious texts. The reading runs across twelve ages of the precessional cycle, from the project's beginning twenty-two thousand years ago to the present age of disclosure and into the long future the next Great Year is opening. The site is free, source-aware, and built so the work can be checked.
